articles.title: Residents evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky reach Ukraine after localized ceasefire
articles.description: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have crossed into Ukrainian-held territory in a significant rescue operation. This happened under the most substantial truce since Russia's invasion of Ukraine over four years ago. The civilians traveled through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump. Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region is expected to continue through Sunday evening. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed U.S. approval of Ukraine’s purchase of 500 Patriot interceptors. Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack killed two people in Russia’s Bryansk region.

articles.title: Civilians from war-ravaged Oleshky arrive in Belarus on their way to Ukrainian territory
articles.description: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine have arrived in Belarus as part of a major rescue operation. This operation took place under the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine over four years ago. Civilians began their journey out of the war-ravaged region in bus convoys on Friday. The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region began on Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening. The estimated 2,000 remaining residents were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

articles.title: G20 foreign ministers to end Atlanta meeting without consensus on key issues
articles.description: Top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies will be wrapping up two days of talks in Atlanta without reaching consensus on several critical global security issues. This is after divisions, notably over Russia’s war with Ukraine, overshadowed the start of the meeting. According to diplomats who attended, the group will not release a joint communique, relying instead on a chairman’s statement summarizing the talks that Secretary of State Marco Rubio will release at the conclusion on Saturday. Rubio canceled the traditional group photo of the foreign ministers on Friday after European diplomats objected to the inclusion of Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

articles.title: Ukraine still finding Swiss components in Russian weapons
articles.description:
Ukrainian authorities continue to find components made by Swiss companies in the wreckage of Russian drones and missiles, reports SRF. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, an adviser to Ukraine’s president on international sanctions, told SRF he wants Switzerland to do more to stop the flow.
Russian military strike drone wreckage found in August 2026 © Ioannaalexa | Dreamstime.com
Ukrainians face missile and drone attacks every night. Mr Vlasiuk describes it as a lottery: anyone could be hit.
Foreign components, chiefly microelectronics, are found in 90% of Russian weapons, he says. Russia’s arms industry is less self-sufficient than it would like to appear. Export controls and sanctions can therefore make a real difference.
Components from Swiss companies are among the most critical, Mr Vlasiuk argues. He says experts who have examined Russian weapons debris since 2022 estimate that 95% of Russian drones and missiles contain parts from Swiss companies, chiefly from STMicroelectronics and u-blox.
STMicroelectronics is a large semiconductor manufacturer headquartered in Geneva, with French and Italian roots and a parent company incorporated in the Netherlands. It makes chips used in cars, industrial equipment and consumer electronics. u-blox is a Swiss technology company that grew out of ETH Zurich in 1997. It makes chips and modules for satellite positioning—such as GPS receivers—and wireless communication.
Ukraine has held extensive talks with the Swiss government, urging it to involve law-enforcement agencies and the export-control authority more closely. Mr Vlasiuk considers the response inadequate. Ukrainian authorities continued to find Swiss components in Russian weapons in September and October.
The Federal Council says it is doing all it can to ensure that companies monitor their supply chains. It also points out that the components are produced and supplied outside Switzerland.
Mr Vlasiuk acknowledges Switzerland’s support for Ukraine but says that explanation might have been acceptable in 2023, not in 2026. Sanctions have evolved, as have Russia’s methods of evading them. The absence of factories or direct exports from Switzerland is, he argues, no excuse for inaction.
The manufacturers say they comply with sanctions and have done no business with Russia since 2022. Mr Vlasiuk points to NXP, a Dutch chipmaker that once attracted even greater criticism. By 2026, he says, Ukrainian investigators were finding almost no trace of its components in Russian weapons. Sustained effort can make a difference; he has yet to see comparable progress from Swiss companies.
Investigations have found that distribution networks in China send electronic components to Russia. Mr Vlasiuk regards China as a problem. Its export-control authority has reportedly announced regulatory changes, which he welcomes, though he doubts their effectiveness.
American chips also remain widespread in Russian weapons. Ukraine works continually with the American government to restrict Russia’s access to them, Mr Vlasiuk says. Even so, American microchips account for an extremely high share of those found in Russian ballistic missiles.
More on this:SRF article (in German)
